title: The body's nature
hookLine: art students draw the skeleton before the skin. some monks went further. two views on why, and how carefully.
tomorrow: is a practice like that meant to make you hate bodies?

lines: THIS BODY TOO IS OF THAT NATURE.
cards: Art students learn to draw the skeleton before the skin; a figure looks wrong until you know what's holding it up. Monks in the old texts went further.

The Satipatthana Sutta describes a monk at a charnel ground, where bodies were left in the open, looking at one over time: newly dead, then picked at by birds, then a skeleton, then scattered bones, then dust.
Each time, he turns back to his own body and reflects: this body too is of that nature. It will become like that. Which is yesterday's question: why would anyone meditate on a skeleton?

teach.b: Buddhaghosa gives the answer a whole chapter: ten foulness subjects, asubha, the stages of a body after death, from swollen to a scatter of bones.
They're medicine, he says, for one temperament in particular, the greedy one, the mind that clings to looks and lust. And here two views open up. The first says: keep it, plainly.

teach.h: KEEP IT: ONE LOOK LOOSENS THE GRIP.
teach.b: Its best case: people cling to bodies, their own and other people's, as if they'll stay young and lovely forever, and one honest look loosens that grip faster than any argument.
A practice isn't wrong just because it's uncomfortable. The second says: handle with great care. Its best case comes from the manual itself.

Buddhaghosa says to go only with a teacher's permission, to tell a senior monk where you're going, to mind the time and the direction of the wind, and he matches the subject to a temperament, not to everyone.
The same Buddha gave other people kindness, or the breath.

teach.h: CAREFUL: A TEACHER, THE RIGHT DOSE.
teach.b: Medicine without the right dose can do harm.
What neither side disputes is the sutta's line: this body too is of that nature. Not a threat.
A fact, held calmly: the body changes.

how: In Theravada tradition the foulness meditations are taught to some monks and lay practitioners by a teacher, matched to temperament; the charnel-ground reflections of the Satipatthana Sutta are recited and studied more widely.

o: bad karma that follows you from one life into the next
the unlovely: a body's stages after death, as a subject
an unlucky omen to avoid before starting a journey

games.q: who says what about the unlovely — tap the pairs.
p: where bodies were left in the open

s: the foulness practice is meant for everyone, all the time
Buddhaghosa matches it to the greedy temperament and says to go with a teacher's permission.
in the Satipatthana Sutta, a monk compares his own body to a body in a charnel ground
this body too is of that nature; it will become like that.
the practice teaches that the body is evil
it's called unlovely to cool lust and clinging to looks; the sutta's line is about change.

games.q: your meditation group debates whether foulness practice belongs in a beginners' class. you lean toward leaving it out. state the other side's best case.
o: it's shocking, and the shock alone is what keeps people awake.
the Buddha taught it, and one honest look loosens the grip of looks.
people long ago saw death all the time, so it felt normal then.
games.why: that's the strongest version: the Buddha's own teaching, and an honest look at change. the careful side's best case is real too: the manual says a teacher, and the right temperament.

practice: Look at one of your hands for a while: the lines, the knuckles, a scar if there is one. Bring to mind how it looked when you were small, and how it may look when you're old.
Rest in that plainly, without picturing anything grim: this hand changes.

wordCard.voice: Asubha: the unlovely, or foulness. Stages of a body after death, held as a meditation subject, with a teacher.

orig.note: Pali: unlovely, not beautiful; usually rendered 'foulness'. The ten stages of a body after death as meditation subjects.

carryVoice: Your line: the body changes. Both sides of the debate agree on that much. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta, the charnel-ground contemplations: a body one day dead … eaten by birds and animals … a skeleton … bones scattered … crumbled to dust; 'this body too is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that')
Visuddhimagga 6 (the ten foulness subjects, the bloated to the skeleton; suited to the greedy temperament; go with a teacher's permission, inform a senior monk, mind the time and the wind direction)
